'''''Gentiana lutea''''', the '''great yellow gentian''', is a species of [[gentian]] native to the [[mountain]]s of central and southern [[Europe]], including the [[Alps]], the [[Carpathians]] (where scarce), the [[Pyrenees]], the [[Apennines]], and the mountains of the [[Balkan Peninsula]]. It is the [[type species]] of the genus ''[[Gentiana]]''.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hitchcock|first1=A. S.|last2=Green|first2=M. L.|title=International Botanical Congress, Cambridge (England) 1930|publisher= Printed under the authority of His Majesty's Stationery Office, by Wyman & sons, Ltd., Fetter Lane, London|location=London|date=1929|page=138|chapter=IV.-Proposal by A.S. Hitchcock (Washington) and M.L. Green (Kew).|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/145068}}</ref>

==Description==
''Gentiana lutea'' is a [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]], growing to {{convert|1|–|2|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall, with broad lanceolate to elliptic glabrous [[leaf|leaves]] {{convert|10|–|30|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|4|–|15|cm|0|abbr=on}} broad, borne in opposite pairs. The [[flower]]s are yellow, 18–24 mm long, with the [[Corolla (flower)|corolla]] separated nearly to the base into 5–7 narrow petals; they are produced in whorls of 3–10 together on the upper part of the stem. Flowering is from June to August. It grows in grassy [[Alpine climate|alpine]] and sub-alpine pastures, usually on [[calcareous]] soils, at altitudes of up to 2500 m.<ref name="Blamey">{{cite book | last1=Blamey | first1=Marjorie | last2=Grey-Wilson | first2=Christopher | title=The Illustrated Flora of Britain and Northern Europe | publisher=Hodder & Stoughton | publication-place=London | date=1989 | isbn=0-340-40170-2 | page=306}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Huxley |first1=Anthony |author1-link=Anthony Huxley |title=Mountain Flowers |date=1967 |publisher=Blandford Press |location=London |page=320}}</ref><ref name="RHSD">{{cite book | last1=Huxley | first1=Anthony | title=Royal Horticultural Society Dictionary of Gardening | publisher=Macmillan Press; Stockton Press | publication-place=London : New York | date=1992 | isbn=1-56159-001-0 | volume=2 | pages=387, 391 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Gentiana+lutea|title=Plants For A Future: Gentiana lutea - L.|accessdate=2025-02-20}}</ref>

==Uses==
[[Image:Gentiana lutea DSCF1627.JPG|thumb|left|Close-up of the flowers; [[Salvan]], Switzerland]]
''Gentiana lutea'' is remarkable for the intense [[bitter (taste)|bitterness]] of the root and every part of the herbage. Gentian was used occasionally in [[brewing]].<ref>{{cite book |title=A Practical Essay on Diseases of the Viscera |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IkQDOfE6cfEC&pg=PR1 |author=Leake, John |year=1792 |page=[https://books.google.de/books?id=IkQDOfE6cfEC&hl=de&pg=PA85#v=onepage&q&f=false 85] |publisher=London: Printed for Evans, Paternoster-Row etc.}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=The Spirit, Wine Dealer's and Publican's Director |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PqVAAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA1 |author=Palmer, Edward |year=1824 |pages=[https://books.google.de/books?id=PqVAAQAAMAAJ&newbks=1&newbks_redir=0&hl=de&pg=PA228#v=onepage&q&f=false 228]-230 |publisher=London: G. and W.B. Whittaker}}</ref>

Gentian root has a long history of use as a herbal bitter and is an ingredient of many proprietary medicines. The parts used include the dried, underground parts of the plant. The root is long and thick, usually about {{cvt|30|cm|0}} long and {{cvt|2.5|cm|0}} diameter, but sometimes 90 cm or more long and 5 cm in diameter, yellowish-brown in colour and very bitter in taste.<ref name=Grieve>{{cite web |url=https://botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/g/gentia08.html |author=Grieve, Maud|author-link=Maud Grieve |title=''A Modern Herbal'' (botanical.com)|accessdate=2025-02-20}}</ref> The rhizome and roots are collected in autumn and dried.<ref name=Grieve/> Caution should be exercised as to its use because it is endangered in some regions,<ref>{{cite journal |last=González-López |first=Oscar  |title=Genetic Variation of the Endangered Gentiana lutea L. var. aurantiaca (Gentianaceae) in Populations from the Northwest Iberian Peninsula |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/262930565_Genetic_Variation_of_the_Endangered_Gentiana_lutea_L_var_aurantiaca_Gentianaceae_in_Populations_from_the_Northwest_Iberian_Peninsula |journal=International Journal of Molecular Sciences |volume=15 |issue=6 |pages=10052–10066 |year=2014 }}</ref>{{citation needed|date=January 2017}} although the species as a whole is not threatened.<ref name="IUCN"/> The related species ''[[Centaurium erythraea]]'' shares many of its constituents and actions.{{citation needed|date=January 2017}}

The name is a tribute to [[Gentius]], an Illyrian king who was thought to have found out that the herb had [[herbal tonic|tonic]] properties.<ref name="RHSD"/>

In veterinary pharmacopeia in the 1860s, gentian root or gentian radix was considered useful as a [[stomachic]].<ref>page 126 of {{Citation | first1=Richard V. |last1=Tuson | last2=Bayne |first2=James | title=A pharmacopoeia including the outlines of materia medica and therapeutics for the use of practitioners and students of veterinary medicine | date=1895 | publisher=Philadelphia P. Blakiston, Son & Co | edition=5th | url=http://trove.nla.gov.au/work/15256665 | accessdate=28 October 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://openlibrary.org/books/OL24167194M/A_pharmacopoeia_including_the_outlines_of_materia_medica_and_therapeutics_for_the_use_of_practitione|title=A pharmacopoeia including the outlines of materia medica and therapeutics for the use of practitioners and students of veterinary medicine|first=Richard V.|last=Tuson|date=February 12, 1895|publisher=P. Blakiston, Son & Co.|ol=24167194M|via=The Open Library}}</ref>

Extracts of gentian root can be found in several liqueurs. It is used in France to produce a number of bitter liqueurs ([[genziana liqueur]]s), including Salers in the [[Cantal]], and a Limousin specialty liqueur and [[aperitif]] called {{ill|Avèze (liqueur)|fr|lt=Avèze}}. The plants are now cultivated in the Auvergne area in view of their protected status, and they are no longer harvested from the wild in the Auvergne mountains.

The [[European Gentian Association]] in [[Lausanne]]<!-- Cercle Européen d'Etude des Gentianacées--> has the objective to develop the knowledge and uses of yellow gentian and other species of Gentianaceae.

{{lang|la|Gentiana lutea}} is depicted on the [[Obverse and reverse|reverse]] of the Albanian 2000 [[Albanian lek|lek]] banknote, issued in 2008. The note depicts [[King Gentius]] on its [[Obverse and reverse|obverse]].<ref>[http://www.bankofalbania.org Bank of Albania]. Currency: [http://www.bankofalbania.org/web/Albanian_banknotes_issue_from_Bank_of_Albania_202_2.php "Banknotes in circulation"]. {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090226154906/http://www.bankofalbania.org/web/Albanian_banknotes_issue_from_Bank_of_Albania_202_2.php |date=26 February 2009 }}. Bank of Albania. Retrieved on 23 March 2009.</ref>

===Chemical constituents===
[[Image:Amarogentin gentiopicrin.png|thumb|right|upright=1.8|Amarogentin and gentiopicrin, the bitter glycosides from gentian root]]
The bitter principles of gentian root are secoiridoid [[glycoside]]s [[amarogentin]] and [[gentiopicrin]]. The former is one of the most bitter natural compounds known<ref>[http://www.awl.ch/heilpflanzen/gentiana_lutea/index.htm "Heilpflanzen: Gentiana lutea"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090902132313/http://www.awl.ch/heilpflanzen/gentiana_lutea/index.htm |date=2009-09-02 }} {{in lang|de}}</ref> and is used as a scientific basis for measuring bitterness.
